title: Real lab: a full git workflow on a real box
instruction: Real Linux box with the real git, no simulation. You are in /root/proj, which holds an untracked file app.txt. Run a complete workflow: (1) git init, (2) git add app.txt, (3) git commit -m 'initial', (4) git switch -c feature (create and switch to a branch), (5) change app.txt and git commit -am 'feature work', (6) git switch main, then (7) git merge feature. Once the feature branch is merged into main, click Verify.
setup: rm -rf /root/proj; mkdir -p /root/proj; cd /root/proj; git config --global user.email lab@example.com; git config --global user.name 'Lab User'; git config --global init.defaultBranch main; echo 'line 1' > app.txt; echo '(scenario ready: an untracked project is in /root/proj, and you are already in it)'

verify.command: cd /root/proj 2>/dev/null; if git rev-parse --verify feature >/dev/null 2>&1 && git merge-base --is-ancestor feature main 2>/dev/null && [ "$(git rev-list --count main 2>/dev/null)" -ge 2 ]; then echo GIT_OK; else echo GIT_NO; fi
verify.success: Solved! init -> add -> commit -> branch -> commit -> merge is the everyday git loop, and you just ran it for real: the 'feature' branch's history is now reachable from main. Branches are cheap pointers to commits; merging simply moves main forward to include them.
verify.fail: Not yet. Make sure you committed on main, created and committed on a 'feature' branch, then switched back to main and merged feature into it. Inspect with: git log --oneline --all --graph

hint: git init; git add app.txt; git commit -m initial; git switch -c feature; echo more >> app.txt; git commit -am 'feature work'; git switch main; git merge feature
